# Statistics and machine learning {#ml}

Statistical models describe how the data arose and estimate the
parameters of that process, with their uncertainty. Machine learning
algorithms look for patterns that predict well, with fewer assumptions
and less interest in parameters. This part explains decision trees and
how a random forest combines many of them.

## 1. Big picture

In statistics we learn about a population from a sample. We write down
a data-generating model (a likelihood), fit it, check it, and report
parameter estimates with confidence or credible intervals. Prediction
often comes second.

In machine learning the goal is usually prediction: find patterns in
the available data that generalize to new cases. The analyst specifies
less, and the algorithm does more of the work. There are no
distributional assumptions about residuals, and relationships needn't
be linear or specified in advance. The price is that there are no
parameters with intervals or p-values to interpret. Machine-learning
predictions can be more accurate than a statistical model's, and the
patterns they find can suggest hypotheses to test with a statistical
model later.

## 2. Decision trees {#trees}

A decision tree is a set of branching rules that predicts a response
from a set of predictors (in machine learning, **features**):

1. Choose the feature, and the split point on it, that divides the data
   into two groups whose responses are as similar as possible within
   each group.
2. Repeat within each group, and again within each of those
   (**recursively**), until a stopping rule is reached, such as a
   maximum depth or too few observations left to split.
3. Predict a new case by following the rules down to a final group (a
   **leaf**) and using that group's mean response (or, for a
   categorical response, its most common class or its class
   proportions).

Each split point is a **node**. A single tree is easy to read, but it
is unstable: a slightly different sample can produce a very different
tree, and a deep tree fits the noise.

## 3. Random forests {#forest}

A random forest grows many trees (500 is a common default), each on a
perturbed version of the data, and averages their predictions:

1. Draw a **bootstrap sample** of the data: $n$ observations drawn with
   replacement from the $n$ in the data set, so each tree sees about
   63% of the distinct observations.
2. Grow a deep tree on that sample. At each node, consider only a
   random subset of the features (in `ranger`, the square root of the
   number of features by default) when choosing the split.
3. Predict by averaging the trees' predictions (for a categorical
   response, by averaging their class probabilities or taking a
   majority vote).

Each tree on its own is a noisy, overfit predictor. Because the trees
see different data and different features, their errors are only
partly correlated, so averaging cancels much of the noise. This is the
same reason a mean of many measurements is more precise than one
measurement.

The observations a tree didn't see (about 37%, its **out-of-bag**
observations) give a built-in test set. Predicting each observation
from only the trees that didn't use it gives an **out-of-bag error**,
an estimate of performance on new data that works like
[cross-validation](Bonus_ModelPerformance.html#cross-validation)
without any refitting.

In the widget, 60 points come from a smooth curve plus noise, with one
predictor. Each tree is grown on a bootstrap sample. (With one
predictor there is no feature subsampling, so this shows the bagging
part of the algorithm.)

```{r forest-widget, echo=FALSE}
widget("forest_average.html")
```

> **Question:** With one tree, how does the step function compare with
> the true curve? Add trees: what happens to the error on new data, and
> why does it level off instead of reaching 0? Then set the depth to 1
> (each tree has a single split). Does averaging still help as much?

# Example: who survived the Titanic? {#titanic}

Passenger records from the Titanic give survival (0 or 1), sex, age,
ticket class, fare, and the numbers of siblings or spouses and of
parents or children aboard. Which features predict survival, and how?

## 1. Data and a single tree {#single-tree}

The data are at
`https://kevintshoemaker.github.io/NRES-746/data/titanic.csv`.
Categorical variables must be factors, not numbers or text, for both
packages used here:

```{r titanic-data}
titanic <- read.csv(
  "https://kevintshoemaker.github.io/NRES-746/data/titanic.csv"
)
features <- c("Pclass", "Sex", "Age", "SibSp", "Parch", "Fare")
titanic <- na.omit(titanic[, c("Survived", features)])   # 714 passengers with known age
titanic$Survived <- factor(titanic$Survived, levels = 0:1, labels = c("died", "survived"))
titanic$Sex <- factor(titanic$Sex)
titanic$Pclass <- factor(titanic$Pclass)       # ticket class 1, 2, 3
str(titanic)
```

A single tree (a **classification tree**; with a numeric response it
would be a regression tree), limited to three levels so it can be read:

```{r single-tree, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
library(party)
tree <- ctree(Survived ~ ., data = titanic,
              controls = ctree_control(mincriterion = 0.85, maxdepth = 3))
plot(tree)
```

Each bar at the bottom shows the share of passengers in that leaf who
survived (dark) and died (light). Sex makes the first split; then class,
and within those groups age or fare. Boys 9 and under in second or
third class survived far more often than older males in those classes,
and nearly all women in first or second class survived. (`ctree()`
grows a *conditional inference* tree, which chooses each split with a
significance test; hence the p-values at the nodes.)

## 2. Fitting a forest {#fit}

`ranger` is a fast implementation of random forests. With
`probability = TRUE` it predicts the probability of each class instead
of a single class; `importance = "permutation"` records the variable
importance described in the next section.

```{r ranger-fit}
library(ranger)
rf <- ranger(Survived ~ ., data = titanic, num.trees = 500, probability = TRUE,
             importance = "permutation", seed = 746)
rf
```

Like most machine-learning algorithms, a forest has tuning settings:
the number of features tried at each split (`mtry`), the minimum leaf
size, and the number of trees. The defaults usually work well. In a
real analysis, try a few settings and compare their out-of-bag error.

## 3. Variable importance {#importance}

**Permutation importance**: for each tree, shuffle one feature's values
among the out-of-bag observations, which breaks its link to the
response, and measure how much the predictions get worse. A feature
the forest relies on loses a lot of accuracy when shuffled.

```{r importance, fig.height=3.5}
imp <- sort(importance(rf))
par(mar = c(4, 7, 0.5, 0.5))
barplot(imp, horiz = TRUE, las = 1, col = "steelblue",
        xlab = "Permutation importance (increase in prediction error)")
```

Sex matters most, then ticket class, fare, and age. Importance says how
much the predictions depend on a feature, not the direction or shape of
its effect, and correlated features (class and fare here) share credit
in ways that are hard to untangle.

## 4. Partial dependence {#partial-dependence}

A **partial dependence plot** shows a feature's effect on the
predictions: set the feature to one value for every passenger, predict,
average, and repeat across a range of values. The other features keep
their observed values, so the curve averages over the real mix of
passengers.

```{r partial-dependence-function}
# mean predicted survival when 'feature' is set to each value in 'values'
partial_dependence <- function(feature, values) {
  sapply(seq_along(values), function(i) {
    nd <- titanic
    nd[[feature]] <- values[i]
    mean(predict(rf, nd)$predictions[, "survived"])
  })
}
```

```{r partial-dependence, fig.width=9, fig.height=5.5}
par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 0.5))
for (f in names(sort(importance(rf), decreasing = TRUE))) {
  x <- titanic[[f]]
  values <- if (is.factor(x)) factor(levels(x), levels = levels(x)) else
    seq(min(x), quantile(x, 0.98), length.out = 30)    # skip the extreme fares
  pd <- partial_dependence(f, values)
  if (is.factor(x)) {
    barplot(pd, names.arg = levels(x), ylim = c(0, 1), col = "steelblue",
            xlab = f, ylab = "Predicted survival")
  } else {
    plot(values, pd, type = "l", lwd = 2, ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = f,
         ylab = "Predicted survival")
    rug(jitter(x[x <= max(values)]))
  }
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

```{r pd-numbers, echo=FALSE}
pd_sex <- partial_dependence("Sex", factor(levels(titanic$Sex), levels = levels(titanic$Sex)))
pd_age <- partial_dependence("Age", c(2, 30))
```

Averaged over the other features, predicted survival is
`r f2(pd_sex[1])` for women and `r f2(pd_sex[2])` for men. Young
children did better than adults (`r f2(pd_age[1])` at age 2,
`r f2(pd_age[2])` at 30), a nonlinear pattern a logistic regression
with a straight-line age term would miss.

## 5. Interactions {#interactions}

If two features don't interact, their two-way partial dependence is the
sum of two separate effects. A simple measure of interaction strength
is how far the two-way partial dependence departs from the best
additive fit:

```{r interaction-strength}
# two-way partial dependence on a grid, and its departure from an additive fit
grid_values <- function(x) {
  if (is.factor(x)) factor(levels(x), levels = levels(x)) else
    seq(min(x), quantile(x, 0.98), length.out = 8)
}
pd_2way <- function(f1, f2) {
  grid <- expand.grid(v1 = grid_values(titanic[[f1]]), v2 = grid_values(titanic[[f2]]))
  nd <- titanic[rep(seq_len(nrow(titanic)), times = nrow(grid)), ]   # every passenger at every grid point
  nd[[f1]] <- rep(grid$v1, each = nrow(titanic))
  nd[[f2]] <- rep(grid$v2, each = nrow(titanic))
  grid$pd <- tapply(predict(rf, nd)$predictions[, "survived"],
                    rep(seq_len(nrow(grid)), each = nrow(titanic)), mean)
  grid
}
pairs <- as.data.frame(t(combn(features, 2)))
names(pairs) <- c("f1", "f2")
pairs$strength <- sapply(seq_len(nrow(pairs)), function(i) {
  g <- pd_2way(pairs$f1[i], pairs$f2[i])
  sqrt(mean(resid(lm(pd ~ factor(v1) + factor(v2), data = g))^2))   # RMS departure from additive
})
pairs <- pairs[order(pairs$strength, decreasing = TRUE), ]
head(pairs, 5)
```

The two strongest interactions both involve sex: sex with class, and
sex with age. Plot them:

```{r interaction-plots, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.8}
# two-way partial dependence: x axis = the feature with more grid values, one line per value of the other
plot_2way <- function(f1, f2) {
  g <- pd_2way(f1, f2)
  if (nlevels(factor(g$v1)) < nlevels(factor(g$v2))) {
    g <- g[, c("v2", "v1", "pd")]
    names(g) <- c("v1", "v2", "pd")
    tmp <- f1; f1 <- f2; f2 <- tmp
  }
  x <- as.numeric(g$v1)
  groups <- split(seq_len(nrow(g)), factor(g$v2))
  plot(NA, xlim = range(x), ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = f1, ylab = "Predicted survival",
       xaxt = if (is.factor(g$v1)) "n" else "s")
  if (is.factor(g$v1)) axis(1, at = seq_along(levels(g$v1)), labels = levels(g$v1))
  for (k in seq_along(groups)) lines(x[groups[[k]]], g$pd[groups[[k]]], lwd = 2, lty = k)
  legend("topright", paste(f2, "=", names(groups)), lwd = 2, lty = seq_along(groups),
         bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 0.5))
plot_2way(pairs$f1[1], pairs$f2[1])
plot_2way(pairs$f1[2], pairs$f2[2])
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Class mattered mainly for women: predicted survival drops sharply for
women in third class but changes little across classes for men. Age
mattered mainly for males: boys survived far more often than men, while
survival declines only gently with age for women. A logistic regression
would need these interactions written in explicitly; the forest found
them on its own.

## 6. Performance {#performance}

How well does the forest predict survival? Compare its predictions for
the passengers it was trained on, its out-of-bag predictions, and
10-fold cross-validation, along with a logistic regression using the
same features. Both models are scored by AUC and McFadden's
pseudo-$R^2$ (both explained on the
[model performance page](Bonus_ModelPerformance.html#auc)).

```{r performance}
y <- as.numeric(titanic$Survived == "survived")
auc <- function(p, y) {
  r <- rank(p)
  n1 <- sum(y)
  n0 <- sum(1 - y)
  (sum(r[y == 1]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}
dev <- function(p) {
  p <- pmin(pmax(p, 1e-4), 1 - 1e-4)       # avoid log(0) for predictions of exactly 0 or 1
  -2 * sum(dbinom(y, 1, p, log = TRUE))
}
mcfadden <- function(p) 1 - dev(p) / dev(rep(mean(y), length(y)))

set.seed(746)
folds <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = nrow(titanic)))
p_cv_rf <- p_cv_glm <- numeric(nrow(titanic))
for (k in 1:10) {
  train <- titanic[folds != k, ]
  test <- titanic[folds == k, ]
  m_rf <- ranger(Survived ~ ., data = train, num.trees = 500, probability = TRUE, seed = k)
  p_cv_rf[folds == k] <- predict(m_rf, test)$predictions[, "survived"]
  m_glm <- glm(Survived ~ ., data = train, family = binomial)
  p_cv_glm[folds == k] <- predict(m_glm, test, type = "response")
}
m_glm <- glm(Survived ~ ., data = titanic, family = binomial)

preds <- list(forest_training_data = predict(rf, titanic)$predictions[, "survived"],
              forest_out_of_bag = rf$predictions[, "survived"],
              forest_10fold_cv = p_cv_rf,
              logistic_training_data = fitted(m_glm),
              logistic_10fold_cv = p_cv_glm)
perf <- t(sapply(preds, function(p) c(AUC = auc(p, y), McFadden = mcfadden(p))))
round(perf, 3)
```

On the passengers it was trained on, the forest looks nearly perfect
(AUC `r f2(perf["forest_training_data", "AUC"])`, pseudo-$R^2$
`r f2(perf["forest_training_data", "McFadden"])`), because its deep
trees memorize much of the training data. Out-of-bag
(`r f2(perf["forest_out_of_bag", "AUC"])`) and cross-validated
(`r f2(perf["forest_10fold_cv", "AUC"])`) AUCs agree, and both are far
lower: never judge a forest by its fit to the training data. Under
cross-validation the forest still beats the logistic regression a
little (`r f2(perf["logistic_10fold_cv", "AUC"])`), in part because it
picks up the age and class patterns the straight-line logistic model
misses.

## Discussion {#discussion}

1. The forest's cross-validated AUC is `r f2(perf["forest_10fold_cv", "AUC"])`;
   the logistic regression's is `r f2(perf["logistic_10fold_cv", "AUC"])`.
   Which would you use to predict survival for a new passenger list?
   Which would you use to explain *why* some passengers survived?
2. Permutation importance ranks fare above age, but fare and class are
   strongly related. What would you need to do to say whether fare
   itself mattered?
3. The partial dependence plot shows a jump in survival for young
   children. How would you write a statistical model to test whether
   that jump is real, and what would it add that the forest can't?
